svg.text: no vendor / no cloud-vs-on-prem decision baked in — every box names a ROLE; red = failure-mode annotation
• routes by path to owning service
⚠ if Customers is down: needs timeout +
⚠ if Requests is down: DocumentUploaded events queue up
durably and are processed once it's back — nothing lost
• no sync call INTO Requests (loose coupling)
• writes metadata + outbox in one transaction
durable queue/topic abstraction — any broker (message broker, log-based
stream, or managed pub/sub); topics: RequestStatusChanged, DocumentUploaded
policy: redelivery lock/visibility timeout + max delivery count per subscription
⚠ if the broker itself is down: publishers must retry/buffer locally (outbox keeps retrying)
sync fallback: fetch recipient if missing
• never queries other services' DBs directly
⚠ if Reporting is down: dashboards go stale — no other
service is blocked; it drains the backlog and catches up on restart
(no consumer depends on Reporting, so it's the cheapest failure in this diagram)
Observability is a CROSS-CUTTING concern, not part of any one domain:
Observability & Alerting (shared, one stack for all 5 domains)
metrics + logs + traces from every service; one rule set, e.g. "any DLQ depth > 0" or "consumer lag > threshold"
(any stack: Prometheus/Grafana/Alertmanager, CloudWatch, Azure Monitor — swappable, same as the broker)
What stays fixed regardless of the chosen stack
1. Transactional Outbox in every publishing service (Requests, Documents)
state update + outbox row are written in ONE local transaction — the event can never be silently lost,
independent of which broker/relay mechanism ships it (polling worker, CDC/log-tailing, or a transactional-outbox library).
2. Async hand-off between domains, never a hard synchronous dependency
Requests, Documents, Notifications and Reporting only talk to each other through events. None of them blocks waiting
Every broker/queue technology can redeliver a message; each consumer (Notifications, Requests, Reporting) de-dupes by
4. Bounded retry → Dead-letter → Alert → Manual replay — a per-CONSUMER pattern, not per-service
Any role that consumes messages needs a DLQ: Notifications and Requests (consuming DocumentUploaded) are critical —
their DLQ pages on-call. Reporting's DLQ is log-only (reviewed periodically, no page) since nothing depends on it staying
fresh. Pure publishers (the Outbox Relays) don't need one — an unsent row just gets retried on the next poll, it's never "dead".
5. Not every dependency is async — sync calls still exist and need an explicit failure policy
Requests→Customers and Notifications→Customers are synchronous reads (marked ⚠ above). A microservice going down
degrades gracefully ONLY where the link is async (queue absorbs the outage). Where the link is sync, the caller needs its
own policy — timeout + circuit breaker, and either a cached/last-known snapshot or a documented degraded behavior —
otherwise a Customers outage silently cascades into Requests and Notifications failing too.
6. Failure blast radius is not uniform across the 5 domains
Reporting going down: nothing else notices (cheapest). Notifications going down: delayed notifications only, protected by
DLQ+alert. Requests or Documents going down: their own inbound writes/API fail immediately (normal sync failure), but
already-published events are safe in the channel. Customers going down is the riskiest because two other services call it
synchronously — this is the one dependency in the diagram that most needs an explicit resilience decision.
Decision left open on purpose: cloud-managed vs. self-hosted broker/storage/observability stack, and which product, is an infra/cost/ops choice — swappable without touching service code.
